Blood test data were traditionally confined to the clinic for diagnostic purposes, but are now becoming more routinely used in many professional and elite high-performance settings as a physiological profiling and monitoring tool. A wealth of information based on robust research evidence can be gleaned from blood tests, including: the identification of iron, vitamin or energy deficiency; the identification of oxidative stress and inflammation; and the status of red blood cell populations. Serial blood test data can be used to monitor athletes and make inferences about the efficacy of training interventions, nutritional strategies or indeed the capacity to tolerate training load. Via a profiling and monitoring approach, blood biomarker measurement combined with contextual data has the potential to help athletes avoid injury and illness via adjustments to diet, training load and recovery strategies. Since wide inter-individual variability exists in many biomarkers, clinical population-based reference data can be of limited value in athletes, and statistical methods for longitudinal data are required to identify meaningful changes within an athlete. Data quality is often compromised by poor pre-analytic controls in sport settings. The biotechnology industry is rapidly evolving, providing new technologies and methods, some of which may be well suited to athlete applications in the future. This review provides current perspectives, limitations and recommendations for sports science and sports medicine practitioners using blood profiling and monitoring for nutrition and performance purposes. http://dx.doi.org/10.13039/100004396 PepsiCo issue-copyright-statement © Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2019 Key Points Introduction Many professional and Olympic-level athlete settings comprise comprehensive sports medicine and sports science support services, with an objective of: (1) achieving the highest possible level of performance with the lowest number of days lost to injury or illness [ 1 ], and (2) a duty of care to protect athletes from long-term negative health consequences of their sport [ 2 ]. A wealth of measurable variables of task-specific performance, training load, physiology, health and wellness exist to facilitate this, which can be used to guide coaches and athletes. In many cases this now includes blood profiling and monitoring, yet there has been no recent review of the practical application of blood profiling and monitoring in sport aimed at this interdisciplinary team. Here, we define ‘blood profiling’ as any blood testing where the data are applied beyond a medical diagnostic or anti-doping purpose. This includes the use of biomarkers to assess the efficacy of training interventions, inform nutritional strategies, and assess the capacity to tolerate training load. We define ‘blood monitoring’ as tests that are conducted frequently (e.g. once per micro-cycle) in order to describe the recovery status of the athlete. There are a host of positive and negative outcome indicators that can be found within the blood that may corroborate or contrast with subjective athlete reports of performance readiness and symptoms, or other objective test data. These can help the practitioner decide whether an athlete is likely to be able to sustain or adapt to training/high performance or to assess the efficacy of an intervention. For example, a high testosterone-to-cortisol ratio suggests greater anabolic drive and has been strongly associated with positive training and performance outcomes [ 3 ]; chronically low energy availability (evident in a reduction in triiodothyronine as an example) reduces the ability to adapt to training [ 4 ], while also being a risk factor for bone stress injuries [ 5 ]; low iron status compromises the erythropoietic effects of altitude linked to endurance performance [ 6 ]; and vitamin D deficiency is known to compromise immunity, muscle repair and bone health [ 7 , 8 ]. The aim of this review is to provide a useful practical guide to blood biomarker profiling and monitoring; it is not intended to be an exhaustive summary of the literature. It is beyond the scope of the present review to discuss sampling of other body fluids such as saliva, urine and tear fluid [ 9 ], or to discuss advanced techniques emerging in sports science such as metabolomics and ‘athleticogenomics’ [ 10 – 12 ]. However, this is not intended to diminish their future importance. Importantly, there are a number of considerations that are often overlooked in the application of blood biomarker measurement in sport, including: (1) consideration given to what is ‘normal’ and what constitutes a meaningful deviation from normal for each individual athlete; (2) pre-testing considerations such as the time of day, posture, fasting/hydration status, transportation and storage of samples, the effects of recent training sessions (i.e. timeline for the restoration of homeostasis for each analyte); (3) sports-specific expertise present to interpret and address actions arising from testing; (4) appreciation of plasma volume shifts where the biomarker is volumetric in nature, e.g. haemoglobin. Screening Versus Monitoring Depending on the frequency of measurement, essentially two approaches can be adopted. The first is screening, i.e. infrequent measurement of selected biomarkers (several months apart) to identify deficiencies or excesses; the second is monitoring, i.e. high-frequency measurement of biomarkers (days or weeks apart) in order to assess ongoing adaptation or recovery (readiness) from disturbed homeostasis. Once enough data have accumulated, sport- (and position-) and athlete-specific reference ranges can be applied. In order to optimise the timing and application of these two approaches, detailed knowledge of the athlete’s training and competition programme is required. While each biomarker provides information about one or more physiological systems, the insights gained are narrow if only a single data point is available. Depending on the sport, sex, and the specific context, an appropriate biomarker or panel of biomarkers can be selected and measured at a suitable frequency. The success of a biomarker screening/monitoring programme depends on a number of factors, including the financial cost, validity and sensitivity (see Tables 1 , 2 ). The usefulness of screening and monitoring with blood biomarkers in providing information that might ultimately reduce injury and illness risk, or impact upon the rate of adaptation to training, is a complex subject. The literature to date will not always provide a clear guide since large randomised, controlled studies of the behaviour of each biomarker are unlikely to ever be possible in these specialised populations. A needs analysis is a logical starting point for undertaking blood biomarker profiling. Over 3 decades of applicable studies of biomarkers in sport, together with extensive medical literature, exist for practitioners to draw upon to enhance decision making. In addition, biomarker technology is rapidly evolving, driven by the colossal biotechnology industry.

extracted_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review discusses the practical application, limitations, and recommendations for blood biomarker profiling and monitoring in high-performance athletes, aiming to optimize physiology, nutrition, training, recovery, and prevent injury/illness. It covers various physiological and procedural factors affecting analysis, the importance of individualized reference ranges, the utility of specific nutritional and stress-related biomarkers (e.g., Omega-3 Index, carotenoids, redox status, glutamine, sex and thyroid hormones, IGF-1, cortisol, iron, tHbmass, inflammatory markers, CK, urea, melatonin, vitamins), and considerations for managing energy availability, training load, and recovery.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Comprehensive Blood Biomarker Profiling and Monitoring for Athlete Management, Nutritional Intervention, and Training Adaptation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The therapeutic approach involves comprehensive blood biomarker profiling (infrequent screening for deficiencies, several months apart) and monitoring (frequent assessment of adaptation/recovery, days or weeks apart) in athletes. This strategy is tailored to individual needs, sport, sex, and training context, utilizing individualized adaptive ranges and critical difference thresholds. It includes careful consideration of pre-analytic factors (e.g., posture, tourniquet use, centrifugation time, time of day, psychological stress, fasting status, menstrual cycle day, hydration status, duration/intensity/mode of prior exercise) and minimizing blood draw volumes, such as the removal of an average of 180 ml (range 82–314 ml) of blood in a simulated altitude study which negated hypoxia-induced erythropoiesis and aerobic performance gains. Specific interventions include targeted dietary/antioxidant supplementation (e.g., Omega-3 to increase OM3I from ~4.5% to ~6%, N-acetylcysteine for low red blood cell glutathione, Vitamin C for low plasma concentrations), iron supplementation for deficiency (e.g., ferritin < 12 ng mL−1 leading to dramatic increases in tHbmass), and nutritional adjustments for energy availability management (e.g., during persistently excessive endurance exercise, 8 weeks of gross energy deficiency, or carbohydrate restriction impacting testosterone/cortisol responses). The monitoring is applied across various contexts like intense exercise, eccentric loading, single matches, long-haul travel, sleep loss, and season-long competitive demands, with biomarker responses proportional to the imposed stress and recovery status.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Iron Status Markers (Iron, Ferritin, MCV, MCH, Reticulocytes, Hepcidin)
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Level/Status, Protein Concentration, Red Blood Cell Parameter, Peptide Hormone Concentration, Deficiency status

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Identification of iron deficiency; low iron status compromises erythropoietic effects. Females are more susceptible due to menstrual blood loss (< 36.5 ml to > 72.5 ml per cycle). Severe iron deficiency is defined as ferritin < 12 ng mL−1. Total hemoglobin mass (tHbmass) is around 40% higher in endurance athletes and can be dramatically increased via supplementation when ferritin < 12 ng mL−1. MCV and MCH provide an indication of compromised erythropoiesis due to iron deficiency. Reticulocyte variables can provide evidence of compromised iron status. Hepcidin shows promise as a highly informative addition to an iron panel; it interacts with exercise, iron deficiency, and iron overload.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Essential for oxygen transport (via hemoglobin in red blood cells), energy metabolism, and metabolic processes. Ferritin is an iron storage protein. MCV and MCH indicate red blood cell volume and hemoglobin content, respectively. Reticulocytes reflect recent erythropoietic activity. Hepcidin regulates iron absorption and systemic iron homeostasis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: High-performance physiology, training interventions, nutritional strategies, altitude training, menstrual blood loss in females, endurance athletes, iron deficiency corrected via supplementation, general health and nutrition screening, RBC data in the context of iron deficiency, monitoring iron status in athletes.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Identification of deficiency; low status compromises erythropoietic effects of altitude and endurance performance, impacting training tolerance. Indicates compromised health and potentially reduced athletic performance due to impaired oxygen transport. Ferritin is a key indicator for iron deficiency, with levels below 12 ng mL−1 indicating severe deficiency requiring intervention. MCV, MCH, and reticulocytes indicate compromised red blood cell production due to iron deficiency. Hepcidin is highly informative for assessing an individual’s propensity to absorb iron. Optimal tHbmass enables greater maximal oxygen-carrying capacity and higher aerobic power; compromised tHbmass indicates sub-optimal aerobic power. Haemoglobin concentration is a poor indicator of true oxygen-carrying capacity (tHbmass) due to susceptibility to plasma volume shifts. Supports athlete health, nutrition, and performance.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Vitamin Status Markers (General Vitamins, Vitamin D, Plasma Vitamin C)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Identification of vitamin deficiency. Vitamin D deficiency (no specific value provided). Plasma Vitamin C: low/high concentrations, increased with supplementation. No explicit quantitative values beyond 'low' or 'high' for specific concentrations in groups, but supplementation increased levels from 'low'.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Diverse roles in metabolic processes, immune function, bone health, muscle repair, and antioxidant defense. Vitamin D is a vital nutritional biomarker. Vitamin C is an antioxidant vitamin.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: High-performance physiology, nutritional strategies, overall health, health and nutrition screening in elite and professional athletes, Vitamin C supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Deficiency compromises immunity, muscle repair, and bone health, potentially increasing injury/illness risk and impacting recovery. Vitamin insufficiencies increase oxidative stress and decrease physical performance. Supplementation improved physical performance in individuals with low plasma Vitamin C, but not in those with high levels. Supports athlete health, nutrition, and performance.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Energy Availability & Thyroid Hormones (Triiodothyronine, free T3, total T3)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Chronically low energy availability, evident in a reduction in triiodothyronine levels. Showed a significant decline in energy-deficient swimmers only; significant changes over time reported during intensified training in male rowers. Marked recovery when nutrition and energy status are restored. Not explicitly quantified but implied changes related to energy availability during intense training.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Regulates metabolic rate, energy balance, and expenditure; crucial for adaptation to training. Bioenergetic hormone, thyroid hormone, offers insight into energy availability.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: High-performance physiology, training load, nutritional strategies, low energy availability, adaptation to training, 12-week training block in energy-deficient female swimmers, intensified training in male rowers, short time frames (e.g., 1 week) with nutritional interventions, intense training period, overall health, nutritional strategies.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates chronically low energy availability, reducing the ability to adapt to training, and is a risk factor for bone stress injuries. Associated with unexplained underperformance syndrome. Indicates energy availability and sensitivity to nutritional interventions. Can be used to ascertain whether timely nutritional adjustments are required to optimize recovery and adaptation with reference to energy availability during intense training.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Oxidative Stress & Redox Status Markers (General, Plasma Antioxidant Response, Red Blood Cell Glutathione)
analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Blood, Blood plasma, Capillary Blood, Red Blood Cell (RBC)
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Status, Response measurement, Level, Activity/Concentration, Level of ubiquitous antioxidant enzyme

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Identification of oxidative stress (no specific quantitative value provided). Response to exercise is a well-established method to assess oxidative stress (OS) and predict adaptation; overloaded athletes display a diminished plasma antioxidant response to an exercise test. Modifiable through diet. Increased exercise-associated lipid peroxidation with exercise (a type of OS biomarker) on a low antioxidant diet. Vitamin insufficiencies increase OS. Significant changes observed in relation to workload across various time points of the season in elite soccer players; periods of oxidative stress (OS) occur in association with periods of higher training loads and competition. OS has been termed a 'molecular switch' for upregulating antioxidant systems. Red Blood Cell Glutathione (GSH): low/high levels (not quantified numerically).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicates imbalance between free radical production and the body's ability to detoxify reactive intermediates; often a response to strenuous physical activity. Regulates oxidative stress and antioxidant defense; acts as a 'molecular switch' for upregulating antioxidant systems for adaptation. GSH is a ubiquitous antioxidant enzyme, involved in redox status.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: High-performance physiology, training load, recovery, exercise test, assessing oxidative stress, predicting adaptation, in overloaded athletes, affected by diet, lifestyle, environment, and training. Low antioxidant diet, vitamin insufficiencies (e.g., vitamin C), intense exercise, imbalance between stress and recovery, overload studies in endurance athletes, single soccer match recovery, various time points of the season in elite soccer, professional rugby, handball, periods of higher training loads and competition, administration of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) to groups stratified by GSH levels.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates physiological stress and potential for cellular damage, which can impact recovery and increase risk of injury/illness. Diminished response indicates adaptation issues or predicts lack of adaptation in overloaded athletes. Increased OS is associated with decreased physical performance. Identifying a blood redox profile can identify individuals whose physical performance may be enhanced through the correction of redox 'deficiency' with appropriate antioxidant treatment. In the 'low' GSH group, NAC improved both aerobic and anaerobic capacity. In the 'high' GSH group, NAC had an adverse effect on aerobic performance. Measuring biomarkers of redox status may aid in individualization and frugal use of antioxidant supplementation. Indicates capacity to train and recover, propensity for successful adaptation, informs recovery needs; identifies maladaptation (performance plateau) and fatigue; associated with healthy adaptation and avoidance of disease when balanced.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Status, Protein Level, Concentration, Response measurement

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Identification of inflammation (no specific quantitative value provided). Responses to controlled treadmill running may differ between healthy and illness-prone athletes. Elevations (cytokines, C-reactive protein) may persist for 24–74 hours post-match depending on the biomarker, recovery time between matches (micro-cycle), playing standard, sex, and position. Lower 24-h C-reactive protein concentrations were observed in healthy college students with an Omega-3 Index above 4% compared to the 'low' Omega-3 Index group (< 4%). No specific numerical values provided for the reduction.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Mediates immune response and tissue repair following injury or stress. Marker of inflammation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: High-performance physiology, training load, recovery, controlled treadmill running (comparing healthy versus illness-prone athletes), exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), single soccer match, post-eccentric exercise recovery in healthy college students with an Omega-3 Index above 4%.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates physiological stress, potential for injury/illness, and informs recovery status, impacting the capacity to tolerate training. Indicator of health status; can differentiate between healthy and illness-prone athletes. Helps assess individual tolerance of training, propensity for successful adaptation, and informs recovery needs. Lower concentrations indicate reduced inflammation and improved recovery post-exercise.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Red Blood Cell & Haemoglobin Parameters (RBC Populations, tHbmass, Haemoglobin Concentration, Blood Cell Counts)
analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Blood, Bone marrow (release) and blood (circulation), Blood sample
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Population Status, Release rate and count, Mass measurement, Protein Level (mass), Cell count, Concentration measurement, Protein Concentration

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Status of red blood cell populations (no specific quantitative value provided beyond general assessment). RBCs are released from bone marrow at > 2 million per second; each cubic milliliter of blood contains 4–6 million RBCs. Small blood losses via phlebotomy are naturally replenished rapidly. Environment- or training-induced gains in total haemoglobin mass (tHbmass) can be reversed with blood loss (e.g., 180 ml phlebotomy to negate hypoxia-induced erythropoiesis). Endurance athletes have around a 40% higher tHbmass than the general population. Blood cell counts are diluted due to hypervolemia associated with endurance training, giving a false impression of anaemia. Haemoglobin concentration is poorly correlated with tHbmass since it is dependent upon blood volume and is susceptible to dilution from plasma volume expansion.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Primary function is oxygen transport throughout the body and maintaining total blood volume, crucial for endurance performance. tHbmass reflects the total oxygen-carrying capacity. Haemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells. Blood cell counts are indicators of blood volume status and oxygen-carrying capacity, used in the diagnosis of anemia.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: High-performance physiology, endurance performance, training interventions, natural physiological processes and blood loss, simulated altitude research study with phlebotomy, endurance athletes, altitude training, iron deficiency, general blood testing in athletes, plasma volume expansion (e.g., with heat acclimation or prolonged exercise), endurance training-induced hypervolemia in athletes.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates oxygen carrying capacity and potential for anemia, which directly impacts endurance performance and the ability to tolerate training load. Essential for maintaining oxygen carrying capacity; rapid replenishment after minor blood losses among non-athletes. tHbmass directly impacts aerobic performance; blood loss can negate aerobic performance gains. Enables greater maximal oxygen-carrying capacity and higher aerobic power; indicates sub-optimal aerobic power if compromised. Blood cell counts can lead to misinterpretation of physiological status, specifically giving a false impression of anaemia when true red blood cell mass may be normal, thus masking or misrepresenting health status. Haemoglobin concentration is a poor indicator of true oxygen-carrying capacity (tHbmass) due to susceptibility to dilution effects.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Anabolic/Catabolic, Stress, Sex Hormones & IGF-1 (Testosterone-to-Cortisol Ratio, Testosterone, Cortisol, Estradiol, Progesterone, IGF-1, Endocrine hormones)
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Hormone Concentration Ratio, Hormone Concentration, Concentration/response measurement, Response pattern

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: High testosterone-to-cortisol ratio (no specific quantitative value provided for 'high'). Testosterone: Values in the lower quartile of the sample, but still within the broad clinical reference range, were associated with a 4.5-fold higher stress fracture rate. Can be influenced by long-haul travel due to a strong circadian effect. Poor energy availability and hormonal suppression (hypogonadism) may occur with persistently excessive endurance exercise and/or inadequate energy intake. Negatively affected by gross energy deficiency across 8 weeks. Carbohydrate restriction can significantly affect responses to intense training. Physiologically relevant changes observed in short time frames (e.g., 1 week), with marked recovery when nutrition and energy status are restored. Significant effects demonstrated under combined stresses (intensified training, sleep loss, energy deficiency) during military basic training. Cortisol: Significant changes over time reported during intensified training in male rowers. Negatively affected by gross energy deficiency across 8 weeks. Carbohydrate restriction can significantly affect responses to intense training. Physiologically relevant changes observed in short time frames (e.g., 1 week), with marked recovery when nutrition and energy status are restored. Significant effects demonstrated under combined stresses during military basic training. Elevated cortisol is associated with sleep loss. Estradiol and Progesterone: Suppressed ovarian hormones were associated with significantly lower energy availability. Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1): Showed a significant decline in the energy-deficient swimmers only. Negatively affected by gross energy deficiency across 8 weeks. Physiologically relevant changes observed in short time frames (e.g., 1 week), with marked recovery when nutrition and energy status are restored. Endocrine hormones: Measurement after submaximal and maximal exercise is more effective in characterizing fatigued states in endurance athletes than measures at rest. Hormonal responses to a two-bout exercise protocol can diagnose overtraining syndrome.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: The Testosterone-to-Cortisol ratio reflects the anabolic (testosterone) vs. catabolic (cortisol) balance in the body, influencing muscle growth, recovery, and stress response. Testosterone is a male sex hormone; plays a role in bone health and overall physiological function, indicating anabolic status. Cortisol is a stress hormone; indicates catabolic status and has a strong circadian effect. Estradiol and Progesterone regulate ovarian cycles and indicate energy status. IGF-1 is a bioenergetic hormone. Endocrine hormones regulate physiological processes, stress response, and metabolism.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Training load, recovery status, performance readiness, athlete population (specifically male athletes with values in the lower end of the clinical range, potentially influenced by congested training and competition schedules), long-haul travel, persistently excessive endurance exercise and/or inadequate energy intake in male athletes, hypogonadism in male Ironman athletes and an elite mixed martial arts athlete, 8 weeks of making weight and gross energy deficiency, intense training with carbohydrate restriction, military basic training, short time frames (e.g., 1 week) with nutritional interventions, 12-week training block in female swimmers with significantly lower energy availability, intensified training in male rowers, submaximal and maximal exercise in endurance athletes, two-bout exercise protocol, sleep loss.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A high testosterone-to-cortisol ratio suggests greater anabolic drive and is strongly associated with positive training and performance outcomes; useful for assessing an athlete's capacity to sustain or adapt to training. Lower testosterone indicates a significantly heightened risk of stress fractures, reflects hypogonadism associated with excessive exercise/energy deficiency, and severe negative effects on endocrine function, health, and performance; demonstrates sensitivity to nutritional interventions. Elevated cortisol indicates stress and recovery imbalance and affects endocrine function, health, and performance. Estradiol and Progesterone's absence of fluctuation is a useful marker of energy status (can be masked by oral contraceptive pill). IGF-1 indicates energy availability, reflects severe negative effects on endocrine function, health, and performance from energy deficiency, and demonstrates sensitivity to nutritional interventions. Endocrine hormone measurement after submaximal and maximal exercise is more effective for characterizing fatigued states. Hormonal responses can be used to diagnose overtraining syndrome. All help assess individual tolerance of training, propensity for successful adaptation, and inform recovery needs.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Nutritional & Dietary Markers (Serum Carotenoids, Plasma Glutamine, GLU/GLN ratio, Serum Calcium, Serum Magnesium, Red Cell Magnesium, Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c), Fatty Acids & Omega-3 Index)
analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Serum, Plasma, Red Blood Cell (RBC) fatty acids, Red Blood Cell (RBC), Blood, Blood spot sample
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Concentration, Ratio of concentrations, Level / Concentration, Percentage of long chain marine fatty acids EPA and DHA as a proportion of total RBC fatty acids, Assessment

measured_effect.direction_of_change: substantially decreased/increased/declined/does not reflect/reflects/significantly lower/significant changes
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Serum Carotenoids: Substantial decreases in resting serum carotenoid concentrations after a 2-week restriction of FV intake. Substantially increased concentrations following increased phytonutrient intake. Declined in asthmatics on a low antioxidant diet. Decreases in response to 'live-high, train-low' training paradigms. No specific quantitative values (e.g., % change, absolute numbers) beyond 'substantial'. Plasma Glutamine: Significantly lower plasma GLN compared to healthy non-fatigued elite athletes. No specific quantitative values provided. Plasma GLU/GLN ratio: Significant changes observed. No specific quantitative values provided. Serum Calcium and Serum Magnesium: Not well suited for blood profiling, stated they do not reflect overall calcium/magnesium status. Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) and Red Cell Magnesium: Not explicitly quantified but stated to reflect dietary exposure over the life of the RBC. Omega-3 Index (OM3I): Mean (SD) of 5.1 (1.0)% in Summer Olympians; 4.9 (1.2)% in Winter Olympians; 4.4 (0.8)% in NCAA Division 1 collegiate footballers. Average 3.7 (1.0)% in vegans; 3.5 (0.7)% in US military servicemembers; median 7.1% in Spanish cohort consuming a Mediterranean diet. Recommended target range: 8–11%. Above 4% vs <4% in healthy college students. Increased from ~4.5% to ~6% in endurance athletes. A relationship was observed within a narrow OM3I range of 2–5% in a military study. General Fatty Acids: Not specified in this context.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Serum Carotenoids are a valid means for assessing fruit and vegetable (FV) intake and are related to antioxidant status. Plasma Glutamine and GLU/GLN ratio are amino acids, whose concentrations are altered by exercise training and training stress. Serum Calcium and Magnesium are generally involved in mineral status. Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) and Red Cell Magnesium reflect dietary exposure over the life of the RBC. The Omega-3 Index assesses omega-3 status, reflects dietary exposure, and omega-3 fatty acids like EPA and DHA are involved in anti-inflammatory responses and membrane fluidity. Fatty acids are components of cell membranes, energy sources, and signaling molecules.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Short-term (2-week) restriction of FV intake (low antioxidant diet), increased phytonutrient (FV, nuts, seeds) intake, 'live-high, train-low' training paradigms, dietary intervention (increase in fruit and vegetable consumption), chronically fatigued elite athletes and acutely fatigued elite athletes, periods of intensified training in national and international athletes, well-trained endurance cyclists, and team sport athletes, nutritional blood profiling, assessment of dietary fat consumption, endurance training, fish/olive oil/fish oil supplementation, post-eccentric exercise recovery, military service, Mediterranean diet, blood spot sample testing, health and nutrition screening in elite and professional athletes.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Decreases in Serum Carotenoids are associated with increased exercise-associated lipid peroxidation, increased ratings of perceived exertion (RPE), and increased resting and exercise inflammatory responses. Increases contribute to enhanced recovery and performance. Can be used to assess compliance and response to dietary interventions. Significantly lower Plasma Glutamine concentrations are observed in fatigued states, suggesting its utility in monitoring. Plasma GLU/GLN ratio consistently showed promise for monitoring training stress. Serum Calcium and Magnesium are not well suited to blood profiling as their serum concentrations do not reflect overall status. Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) and Red Cell Magnesium provide a useful index of global dietary habits. Omega-3 Index above 4% experienced significantly lower post-eccentric exercise muscle soreness (DOMS) at 72 and 96 h, lower 24-h C-reactive protein concentrations, and improved profile of mood states compared to the ‘low’ OM3I group (< 4%). Increasing OM3I from ~4.5% to ~6% enhanced cycling economy in endurance athletes. A relationship was observed between OM3I (2–5%) and cognitive flexibility and executive function, suggesting potential to augment both health and performance. The utility of general fatty acids in sport needs further research to be demonstrated.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Exercise & Metabolic Markers (Lactate, Blood Glucose, Creatine Kinase, Urea)
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Concentration measurement, Protein Level, Protein turnover / Metabolite Level

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lactate is an obvious example of a single biomarker point-of-care test in sport. Blood Glucose is the most common point-of-care test globally. Creatine Kinase: A transient increase can be expected with exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), returning to baseline within 60 hours depending on the physical insult and training status. Athletes routinely have higher concentrations, which may be more pronounced during intense or unaccustomed training (e.g., pre-season training). Urea: Not explicitly stated as a direct change in this context, but monitoring is implied.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Lactate is a byproduct of anaerobic metabolism, related to energy production. Blood Glucose is the primary energy source for the body. Creatine Kinase indicates muscle damage level. Urea indicates catabolic status and protein turnover.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Point-of-care testing in sport, intense exercise, eccentric muscle loading, exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), single soccer match, pre-season training, higher training loads and competition, general monitoring for anabolic or catabolic status in athletes.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Lactate is a common indicator of exercise intensity and anaerobic threshold. Blood Glucose is an indicator of metabolic health and energy availability. Creatine Kinase indicates muscle damage level; helps assess individual tolerance of training, propensity for successful adaptation, and informs recovery needs. Urea helps assess individual tolerance of training, propensity for successful adaptation, and informs recovery needs.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Quantification is limited as it does not provide data on cell function, and cells can migrate from circulation; cells outside circulation (e.g., in skin) are not detected.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Immune response and defense against pathogens.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Quantification alone is insufficient for comprehensive immune status assessment; functional data and consideration of cell migration are needed.
